newsitem.title: JAPAN: Muto says Japan should raise rates by end-1997.
newsitem.headline: Muto says Japan should raise rates by end-1997.

text.p: Cabinet minister Kabun Muto said on Friday that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) should raise interest rates when the economy improves.
He told reporters it would be best to raise rates by the end of 1997.
Muto, director-general of the Management and Coordination Agency, said there was a gap between his view and that of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) on monetary policy.
Referring to recent slow growth in Japan's money supply, Muto said the data reflected the fact that the Japanese economy was suffering from asset deflation.

The BOJ said on Thursday that Japan's broadly defined money supply average of M2 plus certificates of deposit (CDs) grew a preliminary 2.7 percent in March from a year earlier. It grew a revised three percent year-on-year in February.
"A 2.7 percent figure is one when the economy is in a slump. When the economy was in good shape, it used to be around five percent," Muto added.
Muto said Japan should correct its current rock-bottom interest rates, after resolving the asset deflation problem as quickly as possible.

He added that an increase in interest rates would be needed by the end of this year to prevent Japanese capital from fleeing overseas after the revision of the Foreign Exchange Control Laws in April 1998.
Japan's official discount rate currently stands at a record low 0.5 percent.
